query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A conventional Pt‐based catalyst that is subjected to a controlled surface treatment to create a dual-layer structure—with an inner layer exposing catalytically optimal Pt sites for efficient hydrogen adsorption/desorption and an outer self-passivating layer to resist acid-induced corrosion—will demonstrate both enhanced catalytic activity and improved durability for HER and HOR in acidic environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard, untreated Pt or Pt‐alloy catalyst that is highly active for hydrogen reactions but shows gradual performance degradation due to acid corrosion over time.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment (such as selective deposition/etching) designed to reconfigure the surface atomic arrangement in a Pt-based catalyst, thereby exposing optimized active sites while simultaneously promoting the formation of a robust, self-limiting passivation layer.
generation.conditions: Acidic aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 0.5 M H2SO4) under potential cycling conditions representative of fuel cells or electrolyzers.
generation.structural_mediator: A tailored surface/interface composed of a dual-phase structure: an inner layer with active Pt sites optimized for hydrogen adsorption/desorption, and an outer passivating layer that inhibits corrosive attack.
generation.mechanism: Surface/interface engineering modifies the electronic structure and local atomic coordination on the catalyst’s surface. This reduction in hydrogen adsorption overpotential is coupled with the formation of a protective, self-healing passivation layer that mitigates acid-induced degradation, thereby maintaining high catalytic activity and enhancing durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The engineered catalyst is expected to show lower overpotentials and higher current densities for both HER and HOR, along with reduced degradation rates (improved durability) compared to the untreated catalyst.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics obtained from standard, untreated Pt or Pt‐alloy catalysts operated under identical acidic conditions.
generation.boundary: The observed benefits are anticipated to be specific to acidic environments and might not extrapolate to alkaline conditions. Additionally, the overall performance improvement will depend on the precision and reproducibility of the applied surface treatment process.
generation.uncertainty: While the expected improvements in catalytic activity and durability are supported by trends in surface engineering and protective passivation layers in other aggressive environments, the exact magnitude of improvement in electrocatalytic performance under specific testing conditions remains to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set of standard Pt or Pt‐alloy catalysts subjected to the controlled surface treatment to form the dual-layer structure, and a control set of untreated catalysts. Both sets will be tested under identical conditions in 0.5 M H2SO4 with potential cycling to simulate operational environments.
measurements: Overpotential at a fixed current density for HER and HOR
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to evaluate surface passivation
Durability metrics such as percent retention of activity after a defined number of cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-treated catalysts do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in overpotential and Tafel slopes, as well as a lower rate of degradation in catalytic activity compared to the untreated catalysts under identical testing conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: In recent years researchers working with high‐entropy and refractory alloys have shifted focus from solely enhancing mechanical or oxidation‐resistance properties toward controlling surface and microstructural features that improve resilience in extreme environments. Early work primarily explored composition changes and processing routes to achieve superior strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance, often via methods that refine the grain structure (e.g., friction processing or LPBF) and promote the formation of protective surface phases. Although these studies were not performed in electrocatalytic systems, the trend shows that tailoring the material’s composition and surface (or interface) properties can yield a stable, passivated phase even under harsh conditions.
decision.unsolved: While advances in alloy design have succeeded in improving durability in oxidation‐ and radiation‐intensive settings, the specific challenge of realizing an electrocatalyst that is both highly active for HER/HOR and stable in acidic, corrosive environments has not yet been addressed. In particular, how to simultaneously engineer the active sites for optimal hydrogen adsorption/desorption and protect the surface from acid-corrosion remains unclear.
decision.lever: Implementing controlled surface treatment (e.g., precise deposition/etching or selective passivation) to modify the catalyst’s surface atomic arrangement and electronic structure so that highly active sites are exposed while a robust, self-passivating layer forms to impede corrosion in acid
decision.why: Surface/interface engineering offers a direct route to reconcile high catalytic activity with long-term durability. Building on the encouraging strategies seen in high entropy and refractory alloy studies—where tailored microstructures and protective surface phases led to enhanced performance under aggressive conditions—this approach is well suited to adjust the local hydrogen adsorption energetics while providing a barrier to corrosive attack, thus addressing the dual requirements highlighted in the research question.
